scenes.title: The bucket in the outhouse
scenes.caption: The bucket waited in the outhouse behind the attap house.
scenes.body: The bucket waited in the outhouse behind the attap house. Jack Sim was born in 1957 into a poor family in Singapore, the second of three children, and grew up in an impoverished village in Upper Serangoon with no plumbing. Water came from a shared standpipe, and rationing was part of life, with cholera and typhoid moving through the kampong and intestinal worms among children. His father worked as a grocery shop assistant, and the pay could hardly feed three children, their mother and a grandmother. They often wore donated clothes they could not afford to buy. The toilet stood outside. He later summed those years for CNA in 2019: "Life was in an attap house and … the toilet was outside."
scenes.voice: An outside toilet shaped his earliest years.
scenes.turn: His mother was about to open his first school.

quote.text: Life was in an attap house and … the toilet was outside.
quote.speaker: Jack Sim (CNA, 2019)

source.label: CNA Insider, 'From O-level failure to millionaire at 29, on a policy of honesty first' (2019)

scenes.visual: Layered paper cut-out, dusk palette of indigo and kerosene orange. A kampong of attap-roofed houses on stilts among coconut palms; a shared standpipe in the foreground; a small wooden outhouse on a plank walkway. A small boy seen from behind carries a tin bucket toward it. One window glows.

scenes.title: Mother's Business School
scenes.caption: Pancakes cooled on the neighbour's fruit pushcart for three nights.
scenes.body: Pancakes cooled on the neighbour's fruit pushcart for three nights. His mother, Tan Siam Kheng, had first tried selling pancakes through that pushcart, and when they did not sell she gave them away. With her last dollar she took a smocking-cushion class at the community centre, then taught six neighbours the same lesson for a dollar each. Jack, his brother and sister hand-copied her designs from blank exercise books bought at 10 cents into pattern books she sold for two dollars. When smocking went out of fashion she learned makeup at CK Tang, practised on Jack's sister and declared herself a wedding beautician. Over about 25 years she prepared more than 3,000 brides while his brother kept her accounts because she could not read or write. He later said: "I was glad to begin attending “Mother's Business School” at the age of six."
scenes.voice: His mother turned her last dollar into lessons for six neighbours.
scenes.turn: School left him standing outside the door.

quote.text: I was glad to begin attending “Mother's Business School” at the age of six.
quote.speaker: Jack Sim

source.label: Jack Sim, 'Social Entrepreneurship in 1960s Singapore: The Story of My Mother', Skoll (29 Jun 2015)

scenes.title: Outside the classroom door
scenes.caption: He stood outside the classroom while the lesson went on inside.
scenes.body: He stood outside the classroom while the lesson went on inside. At school Jack was talkative and restless, and teachers repeatedly sent him to stand outside the classroom, so he missed lessons. His free textbooks did not arrive until April. He failed his O-levels, then two years later, in 1975, he graduated from vocational school with a hotel-management certificate. On his brother's advice he took work in construction as a site supervisor and was bad at it. The foreman asked his boss to take him off the site. He later told CNA in 2019: "The teacher always asked me to stand outside the classroom, so that was why I always failed."
scenes.voice: He missed the lessons happening behind the door.
scenes.turn: Selling suited him better than supervising.

quote.text: The teacher always asked me to stand outside the classroom, so that was why I always failed.
quote.speaker: Jack Sim (CNA, 2019)

source.label: CNA Insider, 'From O-level failure to millionaire at 29, on a policy of honesty first' (2019)

scenes.title: The S$1.1 million mistake
scenes.caption: The bank called about a bounced cheque.
scenes.body: The bank called about a bounced cheque. Jack had moved into selling building materials, became his department's top salesman, and an investor persuaded him to start his own company. In 1984 he founded Besco Building Supplies. He could not read accounts and only learned cash had run out when the bank called. Soon after he under-priced a Raffles City tender by S$1.1 million. After a week of worry he kept asking himself "just started business and immediately going bankrupt?" Then he confessed the error to the owners, who gave him the contract at the higher price if he used a German manufacturer. In what he calls blissful ignorance he formed a consortium to buy a S$30 million brick factory across the Causeway, then built 14 terrace houses at Rosyth Terrace and a 28-unit block on Meyer Road. He was a millionaire at 29.
scenes.voice: A costly error turned into his first break.
scenes.turn: Then he rushed to save old voices.

quote.text: just started business and immediately going bankrupt?
quote.speaker: Jack Sim, recalling the week

source.label: CNA Insider, 'From O-level failure to millionaire at 29, on a policy of honesty first' (2019)

scenes.title: Reels at Hillview
scenes.caption: The reels sat at Hillview with demolition near.
scenes.body: The reels sat at Hillview with demolition near. Jack learned that Rediffusion's dialect audio archive was still inside the building before it was demolished. A contact offered him everything for a price he later recalled as "You can have everything you want for $2,000." He paid the $2,000 for the archive. He was given only a day to collect it before the building came down. He moved quickly to take away what he could in the time allowed. Years later he donated over 4,700 reels to the National Archives. What had been stored in one building before demolition survived because he acted before the deadline.
scenes.voice: He had a day to save thousands of voices.
scenes.turn: A crisis soon made him question his work.

quote.text: You can have everything you want for $2,000.
quote.speaker: a Rediffusion contact, as Sim recalled in a 2012 oral history

source.label: BiblioAsia (NLB) Jul-Sep 2025, National Archives audio-visual collections

scenes.title: Fifteen houses at half price
scenes.caption: The fifteen properties were suddenly worth half.
scenes.body: The fifteen properties were suddenly worth half. Jack had persuaded developers with a French supplier's clay tiles that a Mediterranean look would lift house prices, and within three years the firm dominated the market. Then the Asian financial crisis forced him to retrench staff and halved the value of his 15 properties, and he held on. He felt useless at work during those months. Around then he heard a speech arguing that a society's graciousness could be measured by the cleanliness of its toilets, and the idea stayed with him. Staff and peers called the toilet idea crazy. In December 1998 he founded the Restroom Association of Singapore. He told his wife that after the recession he would quit business for social work because it felt more fulfilling, explaining at the office: "When I come to the office, I don't feel useful. I feel like a failure."
scenes.voice: Failure at the office pointed him toward toilets.
scenes.turn: He decided to take toilets worldwide.

quote.text: When I come to the office, I don't feel useful. I feel like a failure.
quote.speaker: Jack Sim

scenes.title: Mr Toilet
scenes.caption: Laughter greeted the word toilet.
scenes.body: Laughter greeted the word toilet. On 19 November 2001 Jack founded the World Toilet Organization, and its founding date became World Toilet Day. Talking about toilets was taboo and people laughed at him, so he made toilet humour his brand and became known as Mr Toilet. He told audiences in figures he often repeated: "We go to the toilet six to eight times a day and spend three full years of our lives inside the toilet" In 2004 he stepped down as chief executive of Besco, his first company, to give the cause most of his time. The jokes opened rooms that polite language had not opened, and he kept using them.
scenes.voice: He laughed first so others would listen.

quote.text: We go to the toilet six to eight times a day and spend three full years of our lives inside the toilet
quote.speaker: Jack Sim (Tatler Asia, 2020)

scenes.title: The bank that said no
scenes.caption: The award arrived in 2008.
scenes.body: The award arrived in 2008. TIME named Jack one of its Heroes of the Environment. In 2011 he founded the BoP Hub to design businesses for the world's poorest. Donors still avoided the brown issue, and one of Asia's biggest banks told him funding him would hurt its image. He kept working without pay, and by 2022 he had worked unpaid for 21 years because donors avoided the issue. The recognition widened the rooms he could enter but did not pay a salary. He pushed faster anyway, living by the rule he gave in 2022: "Life is short. Every day is one less, so we need to be working faster"
scenes.voice: A bank praised his work and turned him down.
scenes.turn: Then the world gave toilets a day.

quote.text: Life is short. Every day is one less, so we need to be working faster
quote.speaker: Jack Sim (Splash Projects, 2022)

scenes.title: A day at the UN
scenes.caption: The resolution passed on 24 July 2013.
scenes.body: The resolution passed on 24 July 2013. That day the UN General Assembly adopted Singapore's Sanitation for All resolution, making 19 November UN World Toilet Day. Tatler counted 122 countries that co-sponsored it. That same year the World Toilet Organization was granted consultative status with the UN Economic and Social Council. He welcomed the decision in plain words he used that July: "There is nothing wrong with going to the toilet." The date gave the cause a place on the calendar, and the status gave his group a standing that let it keep returning to the same rooms.
scenes.voice: A local date became a world date.
scenes.turn: Cameras soon followed him across continents.

quote.text: There is nothing wrong with going to the toilet.
quote.speaker: Jack Sim (Eco-Business, Jul 2013)

scenes.title: Mr. Toilet on film
scenes.caption: The scooter rolled into frame.
scenes.body: The scooter rolled into frame. Filmmaker Lily Zepeda followed Jack for five years across Singapore, India, China and the United States for Mr. Toilet: The World's #2 Man. On screen he rode a scooter, combed his hair with a toilet brush and swam with a poo-emoji float. The film also showed tension with some WTO board members. At home his collection of toilets appeared in CNA's Money Mind profile. The documentary premiered at Hot Docs, North America's largest documentary festival, in April 2019 and opened in New York on 22 November 2019. The humour stayed on camera, but the strain behind the work stayed there too.
scenes.voice: He combed his hair with a toilet brush on camera.
scenes.turn: An old report card got a new reading.

scenes.title: The boy outside the door, again
scenes.caption: The suggestion came from his daughter.
scenes.body: The suggestion came from his daughter. At about 65 Jack's daughter, a psychology student at SMU, told him she thought he had ADHD. He began to read his schoolboy restlessness differently after years of talk and restless energy at school. That same year the University of Strathclyde awarded him an honorary doctorate. He framed the lesson he would give his younger self in words he later repeated: "his quirks were actually his strengths" At home he lived with his wife, whom he married in 1990 after a first marriage in 1989 ended in divorce after a year, and their four children, two sons and two daughters. The restless boy and the honorary doctor were the same person.
scenes.turn: He still kept dozens of jobs going at once.

quote.text: his quirks were actually his strengths
quote.speaker: Jack Sim, on what he would tell his younger self

checked.note: Quote is his, daughter who studied psychology at SMU suggested ADHD at 65, born 1957 with 2022 Strathclyde honorary doctorate, first marriage 1989 ended after a year and remarried 1990 with two sons and two daughters

scenes.title: Eighty projects at once
scenes.caption: The centre rose in Kampong Ubi.
scenes.body: The centre rose in Kampong Ubi. Jack built a S$10 million, 65,000 sq ft centre there, renamed the SDG Centre and financed mostly by a bank loan. Inside it held a kitchen to train single mothers. At 68 he said he ran 80 to 100 projects at once and lived with his wife and four children. The building gave his many projects one address. The kitchen gave single mothers a place to learn. The household gave the pace of those years a private shape, with work and home staying close together through long days.
scenes.turn: The kitchen light stayed on after hours.
scenes.visual: Paper-layered cutaway of a big industrial-estate building, floor by floor: co-working desks, a training kitchen with ovens, an event hall. On the ground floor a man seen from behind holds a door open. Morning light.
